In any event, notoriety is an unreliable measure of social importance. 
Administrative adjudicators make thousands of decisions every day that 
affect the central interests of ordinary people. These decisions are 
incredibly important to the individuals affected and, when considered in 
the aggregate, to society as a whole. A few arenas of such high-volume, low- 
visibility, mass administrative justice involve decisions about whether to:
• 
Authorize the payment of Social Security retirement benefits;
• 
Grant a disability pension;
• 
Provide Medicaid benefits;
• 
Issue a professional license; or
• 
Grant asylum protection or order a person deported from the 
United States.
Even many routine, lower-stakes decisions fall within the definition of 
“adjudication,” such as when the Forest Service grants a permit to cut and 
take a Christmas tree from a national forest or the Postal Service 
determines whether a letter or package has sufficient postage. The world 
of administrative adjudication is vast and varied!
Administrative adjudication is a concept of such enormous breadth in 
part because of the way the federal Administrative Procedure Act (APA) 
defines it. The APA divides all agency action into two mutually exclusive 
categories: rulemaking and adjudication. The definitions of these terms are 
grounded in concepts of, respectively, quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial 
government action, which were developed by the courts as a matter of 
constitutional due process long before the APA was enacted. The APA 
draws upon these concepts and also defines “adjudication” as a catch-all for 
any agency process that produces a final disposition in a matter that is not 
“rulemaking.” We turn to the subject of rulemaking in Chapter 5. But 
historically, conceptually, and as a matter of statutory interpretation, one 
cannot understand adjudication without having some basic understanding 
of rulemaking. Another foundational necessity is understanding the 
constitutional limitations on Congress’s ability to commit matters to 
adjudication by agencies rather than by Article III courts.
Should the vast array of different decisions produced through 
adjudication be made using a single, uniform set of procedures? The law 
gives a clear answer: “no.” Beyond this rare bit of clarity, determining the 
procedural requirements applicable in any given adjudication is messy 
business. Such requirements are found in various sources: constitutional 
due process, the APA, the agency’s organic statute, and the agency’s own 
regulations. A competent administrative lawyer must understand each of 
these pieces and appreciate the subtle and complex interactions among 
them.
